paras.text: The halogen atom is a good leaving group and detaches from carbon atom, with its bonding electron pair to form a stable halide ion. When a nucleophile attacks on α–carbon and replaces the halide ion, the reaction is a nucleophilic substitution. When the halide ion leaves along with another atom (often H) from the adjacent carbon atom, it forms a new pi bond, the reaction is an elimination. In elimination reactions, a molecule of HX is lost from the alkyl halide to give an alkene. These elimination reactions are called dehydrohalogenation (Section 16.5.5.2), because a hydrogen halide has been removed from the alkyl halide. Substitution and elimination reactions often compete with each other (Section 17.1.8).

The halogen atom is a good leaving group and detaches from carbon atom, with its bonding electron pair to form a stable halide ion. When a nucleophile attacks on α–carbon and replaces the halide ion, the reaction is a nucleophilic substitution. When the halide ion leaves along with another atom (often H) from the adjacent carbon atom, it forms a new pi bond, the reaction is an elimination. In elimination reactions, a molecule of HX is lost from the alkyl halide to give an alkene. These elimination reactions are called dehydrohalogenation (Section 16.5.5.2), because a hydrogen halide has been removed from the alkyl halide. Substitution and elimination reactions often compete with each other (Section 17.1.8).

Tidbit

Besides alkyl halides, many other types of compounds undergo substitution and elimination reactions. Substitutions and eliminations are introduced in this unit using the alkyl halides as examples. In unit 18, we encounter substitutions and eliminations in alcohols.

The strength of carbon–halogen bond decreases down the group from fluorine to iodine. This can be explained on the basis of their bond energies that are given in the Table 17.1. The table shows that iodo compounds are most reactive while fluoro compounds are least reactive. Therefore, the reactivity of alkyl halides increases from fluorine to iodine and the reactivity order is; R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F.

17.1.6 Nucleophilic Substitution (SN) Reactions

17.1.6.1 General Introduction

Alkyl halides undergo nucleophilic substitution reactions in which a stronger nucleophile replaces the halide ion (Section 16.1.5). A general example of such a reaction is given as;

Alkyl halides undergo nucleophilic substitution reactions by two different types of mechanisms i.e. unimolecular (SN1) and bimolecular (SN2) nucleophilic substitution.

17.1.6.2 Important Concepts

17.1.6.2.1 Substrate and Leaving Group

The molecule which undergoes nucleophilic substitution reaction is called substrate. The group or species which leaves the substrate or which is being replaced by the incoming nucleophile is called leaving group or nucleofuge. In the above reaction, alkyl halide is substrates and halogen (halide ion) is the leaving group.

17.1.6.2.2 Nucleophile and Base

Any species neutral or negatively charged with an unshared pair of electrons can act both as a base and a nucleophile. Nucleophile is a species which donates electron pair to an electrophilic center in a molecule and undergoes nucleophilic substitution or addition reactions. A nucleophile is generally represented by N̈u. The strength of nucleophile is called nucleophilicity and is a measure of how fast a nucleophile displaces a leaving group from a suitable substrate.

But a base is a species which has affinity for proton, and donate electron pair to a proton in a reaction, and generally represented by B̈. Base give elimination reaction in alkyl halides. The strength of base is called basicity and represented in terms of equilibrium constant for abstraction of a proton.

17.1.6.2.3 Carbocations and their Stability

A carbocation is an ion in which a carbon atom has a positive charge and three bonds. Carbocation is formed when an electrophile adds to carbon-carbon double bond or when halogen atom detaches from the carbon atom of an alkyl halide as halide ion. The positive carbon of alkyl carbocation is sp²-hybridized and has trigonal planar structure, with empty unhybridized p orbital perpendicular to the plane, as shown in (Figure 17.2).
